questions.q: Who delivers the letter to the Reverend Stephen Kumalo?
choices: A small child sent from the store
questions.explain: A small child runs 'importantly' to the wood-and-iron church with the letter from the store.

questions.q: From which city does the letter come?
questions.explain: The letter is postmarked Johannesburg, where many of Kumalo's people have gone.
It is signed by the Rev. Theophilus Msimangu of the Mission House, Sophiatown.

questions.q: What does the letter ask Kumalo to do?
choices: Come quickly to Johannesburg because his sister is very sick
questions.explain: Msimangu writes that Gertrude Kumalo is very sick and asks Kumalo to come quickly.

questions.q: Why had Kumalo's sister Gertrude originally gone to Johannesburg?
choices: To look for her husband, who never came back from the mines
To sell goods at a market
questions.explain: Gertrude took her small son to look for the husband who had been recruited for the mines and never returned.

questions.q: What money do Kumalo and his wife decide to use for the journey?
choices: The St Chad's money saved to send their son Absalom to school, plus the Post Office savings
questions.explain: They break into the tin of St Chad's money (about twelve pounds) and the Post Office Book with ten pounds saved for a stove.

questions.q: What had the ten pounds in the Post Office Book been saved for?
questions.explain: 'I have been saving that for your stove,' Kumalo says; his wife tells him to take it anyway.

questions.q: What is Kumalo's brother John's trade in Johannesburg?
questions.explain: John Kumalo is a carpenter with a business of his own in Sophiatown.

questions.q: Why had Kumalo's son Absalom gone to Johannesburg?
choices: To look for his aunt Gertrude
To work in his uncle John's shop
questions.explain: Absalom went to look for his aunt Gertrude 'and he had never returned,' nor written.

choices: With Kumalo going to pray in the church while his wife sits with her head on the table
With a letter from Absalom arriving
questions.explain: Kumalo says he will pray in the church; his wife bows her head on his table 'with the patient suffering of black women.' 'All roads lead to Johannesburg.'
